events.title: Nimitz encounter — November 2004
events.summary: David Fravor later testified that he saw an unusual object during a Navy training deployment near the USS Nimitz in November 2004. His visual account, radar information reported to him and a later crew’s infrared recording are distinct evidence.
events.significance: The encounter, its later testimony and the release of related footage are different events.
established: Fravor’s 2023 prepared statement and testimony record his firsthand visual account.
His statement relays radar information from ship personnel and describes a different crew subsequently recording infrared footage.
limitations: No raw radar data or calibration were inspected for this entry. The later film is not a recording by Fravor of his own encounter.
Testimony establishes what the witness reported; it does not independently measure extraordinary performance or establish origin.

events.title: Aristotle argues for a single cosmos
events.summary: In On the Heavens, Aristotle organised the cosmos through arguments about natural bodies and their motions. He distinguished circular heavenly motion from terrestrial motions and argued that the universe contains all available matter, leaving no material for additional worlds. This entry records a philosophical model and its reasoning, rather than an observational demonstration of cosmic uniqueness.
events.significance: A chronology of knowledge includes durable frameworks that were later challenged; Aristotle's account makes the premises behind one influential picture of the heavens open to inspection.
established: Book I distinguishes circular and straight natural motions.
Book I, parts 8–9, argues that there is only one heaven or cosmos.
limitations: The surviving argument is historical natural philosophy, not evidence that only one planetary system exists.
The approximate date cannot be resolved to a precise year or day from the inspected text.

events.title: Epicurus reasons about innumerable worlds
events.summary: Epicurus's Letter to Herodotus argues that infinite atoms and space permit innumerable worlds, some similar to ours and some different. The argument belongs to an atomist account of nature preserved in the ancient textual tradition. It demonstrates that a plurality of worlds was thinkable long before instruments could establish the existence of planets around other stars.
events.significance: The letter distinguishes the history of possible worlds from their detection, giving readers a clear example of a speculative argument that predates observational tests.
established: The letter explicitly argues for infinitely many worlds, including worlds unlike ours.
Its stated basis is an argument about atoms and infinity, not telescopic evidence.
limitations: Ancient ‘worlds’ cannot be equated without qualification with modern exoplanets.
Neither a precise composition date nor evidence of extraterrestrial life follows from this passage.

contextLinks.note: The texts offer contrasting historical positions, without demonstrating direct transmission between them.

events.title: Aryabhata explains apparent stellar motion
events.summary: The Aryabhatiya combines mathematical rules with an account of astronomical cycles. In a famous comparison, a traveller in a moving boat sees stationary objects move backward, just as an observer sees stars move westward. The text supports an Earth-rotation interpretation, although adjacent verses and later commentaries complicate reconstruction of the author's complete cosmological system.
events.significance: This entry broadens the history of mathematical astronomy and shows why precise readings matter: a rotating Earth is a specific proposal, not automatically modern heliocentrism.
established: Golapada stanza 9 uses a moving-boat analogy for apparent westward stellar motion.
Kalakriya stanza 10 supplies the conventional 499 CE epoch.
limitations: The following stanza has a conflicting-looking account; the inspected translation discusses this textual difficulty.
The text locates Earth centrally and must not be presented as the modern Sun-centred planetary system.

events.title: Ibn al-Haytham investigates light and vision
events.summary: In the Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham examined competing explanations of vision and argued that light and colour from visible objects affect the eye. His investigation combines geometrical reasoning with controlled arrangements and repeated inspection. The opening methodological discussion treats investigators as fallible and calls for criticism of assumptions as well as careful observation.
events.significance: The work connects theories of perception to inspectable procedures, adding an Arabic scientific tradition to the chronology without reducing a cumulative history to one inventor.
established: Book I examines whether vision depends on something coming from objects to the eye.
The work describes controlled viewing arrangements and an explicitly critical investigative procedure.
limitations: The entry does not claim that Ibn al-Haytham invented experimentation or the scientific method.
Only the specified direct-vision passages are assessed; this is not a validation of the whole historical optical system.

events.title: Shen Kuo records magnetic-needle behaviour
events.summary: In Dream Pool Essays, Shen Kuo describes magnetised needles that tend to point south while deviating slightly eastward. limitations: This is not a claim that Shen Kuo invented the compass or discovered every aspect of magnetic declination.

events.title: Copernicus publishes a Sun-centred planetary system
events.summary: De revolutionibus placed Earth among the planets moving around the Sun and explained the daily appearance of the heavens through Earth's rotation. Copernicus presented a mathematical reordering of an inherited astronomical problem. Its publication also depended on Rheticus carrying the project forward and Johannes Petreius's Nuremberg press, while an anonymous preface complicated how readers encountered the argument.
events.significance: The book changed the arrangement under discussion and made it available for calculation and criticism; publishing a model and establishing all its claims remained different tasks.

limitations: The book's historical planetary model should not be equated in every detail with current astronomy.

events.title: Kepler publishes a revised orbit for Mars
events.summary: In Astronomia nova, Johannes Kepler used Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars to test and revise planetary models. The resulting account replaced a circular orbit for Mars with an ellipse and addressed changing orbital speed. The published work preserves an extended process of mathematical trial and correction, rather than a single observation that immediately revealed the answer.

events.title: Galileo publishes telescopic observations
events.summary: Sidereus nuncius reported observations made with Galileo's improved telescope: an uneven lunar surface, numerous previously unseen stars and changing points of light near Jupiter. The book also acknowledges news of a telescope made elsewhere, placing his observations within a developing craft of optical instruments.
events.significance: The publication made new observations available for checking and debate, while showing that instruments extend perception through an interaction of manufacture, repeated use and interpretation.

events.title: Descartes publishes his Discourse on Method
events.summary: In Discourse on Method, René Descartes described a personal programme for directing inquiry. Its four precepts call for careful assent, dividing difficulties, moving in order from simpler matters to more complex ones, and checking completeness. The work presents a proposed discipline of reasoning within a wider philosophical project, rather than a neutral manual already shared by all investigators.

events.title: Newton publishes the Principia
events.summary: Newton's Principia set out laws of motion and a mathematical treatment of gravitational attraction, connecting terrestrial and celestial problems within one framework. events.title: Faraday demonstrates electromagnetic induction
events.summary: Using an iron ring wound with separate coils, Michael Faraday found that changing the current in one circuit produced a brief electrical effect in the other. His subsequent report compared arrangements involving coils and magnets. The important feature was change: establishing or interrupting a magnetic condition could induce a current without a direct electrical connection between the circuits.
events.significance: The experiment made a new relationship between electricity and magnetism measurable, with apparatus and repeatable changes connecting an observed effect to later mathematical accounts.
established: The preserved ring apparatus is associated with the experiment of 29 August 1831.

limitations: The date marks one documented experiment within a continuing programme of investigation.

events.summary: The Linnean Society received a joint communication containing Charles Darwin's earlier writings and Alfred Russel Wallace's independently developed essay on species change. events.title: Maxwell publishes an electromagnetic theory of light
events.summary: Maxwell's A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field described interacting electrical and magnetic processes and derived a wave account of light. He compared the calculated propagation speed with independent electrical measurements and measurements of light's speed. The argument explicitly built on experimental work, including Faraday's, while expressing parts of its explanation through the mechanical-medium ideas of its period.
events.significance: The paper linked apparently different phenomena through a quantitative theory, showing how agreement between independent measurements can strengthen an explanation while its conceptual machinery continues to change.
established: Part VI compares electromagnetic propagation with measured light speed and identifies light as an electromagnetic disturbance.
The paper explicitly discusses Faraday's experiments and induction.
limitations: The paper's mechanical-medium assumptions belong to its historical formulation and should not be silently presented as current requirements.
The publication is a theoretical account, not the later experimental production and detection of radio waves.

Unidentified is a case classification; it does not establish a particular craft, performance or origin.

events.title: Phoenix Lights — moving formations and a later flare display
events.summary: Arizona witnesses reported moving lights during the evening of March 13, followed around 10 p.m. by a separate row of lights southwest of Phoenix. Accounts differed about whether the earlier lights formed one solid object. Contemporary telescope testimony supported aircraft; military flare drops and later analyses explain the widely recorded later display.
events.significance: A landmark public controversy shows why a memorable case name can conceal different observations. Explanations need to match the particular time, location and evidence.
established: NUFORC’s preliminary 1997 compilation records moving-formation reports across Arizona and cautions that its account preceded written submissions.
In June 1997, Tony Ortega reported that amateur astronomer Mitch Stanley resolved separate aircraft through a telescope. This is a reported visual observation, not a preserved telescope image.
Ortega’s 1998 investigation separately reports military confirmation of a roughly 10 p.m. flare drop. It quotes a Maryland spokesman saying those aircraft did not fly north of Phoenix.
McGaha and Nickell’s 2015 assessment argues for aircraft in the earlier formation and describes McGaha’s interview with the later flare-flight leader. Portions repeat the earlier reporting.
limitations: Neither the later flare explanation nor the aircraft account establishes the identity of every reported light. No calibrated raw imagery, complete flight logs or independent reconstruction was inspected here.
Witness recollections differ in perceived size, height and solidity. Unresolved details do not establish a non-human craft.
A 2026 internet-questionnaire paper concerns respondents’ remembered experiences and attitudes. Only its abstract was inspected; it does not supply a physical identification.
openQuestions: Which contemporaneous flight and observation records can securely match the earlier reports to particular aircraft?
events.dateNotes: Incident date uses Arizona local time. The NUFORC summary is dated August 13, 1997; contemporary newspaper reporting and later assessments have their own publication dates. The documentary premiere belongs to 2005, not the 1997 incident.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki — the human cost of atomic weapons
events.summary: The United States used atomic bombs against Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9. The attacks killed large numbers of people and left survivors with injuries and lasting social consequences. The same nuclear physics that opened a new field of knowledge had been organized into weapons used against cities.
events.significance: A history of expanding capability must also confront destructive uses, survivors’ experiences and responsibility. Scientific consequence is not moral endorsement.
established: DOE’s chronology dates the Hiroshima and Nagasaki attacks separately.

limitations: This compact entry does not adjudicate every competing explanation of Japan’s surrender or the historical debate over alternatives.
No single precise casualty total is imposed; estimates depend on the period and consequences counted.

changeLog.title: Initial source audit
changeLog.detail: Separated the December 16, 2017 online story from its December 17 print-front-page appearance. Earlier summaries are research leads, not sources.

changeLog.title: Removed an unsupported September 4 transfer date
changeLog.detail: NARA’s page-review date does not establish when additional agency collections arrived. The current eight-agency listing is described as a checked holding, not a newly dated transfer event.

changeLog.title: Narrowed the archive-procurement claim
changeLog.detail: Readable reporting supports an intended purchase, not an award. The previously stated July 31 notice date was not verified and is not used.

changeLog.title: Kept the waiver’s scope explicit
changeLog.detail: The announcement concerns specified communications to PURSUE. It is not described here as general permission for public disclosure.

changeLog.title: Added a historical NASA meeting
changeLog.detail: Added NASA’s May 31, 2023 public study meeting after inspecting the agency’s record. This is a historical addition, not a new incident or a finding about UAP origins.

changeLog.title: A historical layer, with provenance kept visible
changeLog.detail: Added selected historical milestones and a sourced people/programs index. Modern disclosure remains the default. The Maison Rouge report is an attributed intelligence account; UBC and BBH remain distinct; Gateway is Army-authored; Magenta sorts on a verified later retelling rather than an unverified 1933 crash. AIR’s final review is distinguished from its earlier draft. These are historical additions, not new incidents.

changeLog.title: Religious texts and channeling: a distinct historical strand
changeLog.detail: Added Nag Hammadi composition/copying context, the uncertain burial history, 1945 discovery, editions and translation milestones; plus a dated guide to the original Ra books, final session and later editions. Ancient ranges remain approximate, channeling claims remain attributed, and no historical connection between the two is asserted. These are historical additions, not newly occurring UAP incidents.

changeLog.title: Historical breadth and clearer evidence boundaries
changeLog.detail: Added 28 bounded historical, international, scientific and records milestones; corrected document/release dates, added original transcripts and reports, separated core/contextual layers from eras, and documented source inspection scopes. The broad research cutoff and scheduled-reporter status are unchanged.

changeLog.title: A chronology of people, discovery and encounters
changeLog.detail: Introduces an all-era main reading path, dated human contributions, bounded landmark encounters including Phoenix Lights, and deep-time/BCE navigation. Supporting records retain their original anchors. Evidence limits, previous corrections, source identities and reporter settings are preserved.

changeLog.title: Institutional chronology and acronym dossiers added for review
changeLog.detail: Added source-scoped formation, transition and disclosure records, a separate institutional chronology and canonical organization dossiers. Main history and stable anchors retained. Research centers, operators, systems and agencies are distinguished. This local revision has not been published.

navy-nisc-notice-20261012.scope: Errata under Facilities Modified, following January 1973 shore establishment list
navy-nisc-notice-20261012.basis: Corrected contemporary notice lists July 1, 1972 combination/redesignation of scientific/technical and reconnaissance support centers as NISC.

navy-niwc-rename-20261012.basis: Atlantic and Pacific Systems Centers become NIWCs effective February 18, 2019; missions retained.

navy-nmic-thesis-20261012.scope: Abstract and selected institutional-history passages, not all 84 PDF pages.
navy-nmic-thesis-20261012.basis: January 14, 2009 establishment reported by Navy lieutenant; 2009 ONI centers. Author expressly disclaims official-policy status.

navy-nmio-about-2012-20261012.scope: Archived September 13, 2012 page; archive capture is not document creation date.
navy-nmio-about-2012-20261012.basis: National intelligence integration role; NMIC houses ONI, Coast Guard ICC and NMIO staff.

navy-nmio-rename-20261012.basis: January 2009 establishment through ICD 902; January 23, 2012 announced rename from NMIC to NMIO; facility keeps NMIC name.

navy-nrl-centennial-20261012.basis: 1923 commissioning, circa-1926 shortened name, 1946 ONR administrative transfer, early radio and sound work.

navy-nsg-lineage-20261012.basis: 1935 Communication Security Group, 1950 NSG designation, 1968 command designation, 2005 disestablishment.

navy-nuro-csi-review-20261012.scope: Publication pages 55 and 68 read in full text mirror. CIA PDF URL returned 404. This is primary evidence of a public reference, not primary evidence for operational allegations within the reviewed book.
navy-nuro-csi-review-20261012.basis: September 2023 publication includes a book-review reference to NURO; disclaimer rejects official endorsement of authors’ facts or interpretations.

navy-nuro-inman-20261012.scope: Selected NURO and oversight passages; eleven listed interview sessions October 2021–January 2022. Publication date is not assigned as the interview date.
navy-nuro-inman-20261012.basis: Inman identifies himself as NURO director; recalls technology acquisition separately from Navy/NSA mission execution. Public transcript, not declassification order.

navy-nuro-nsdm40-20261012.scope: Two-page NSDM within an 84-page 1976 packet. Neither packet date nor a partly legible declassification stamp is treated as the Program’s formation/public release date.
navy-nuro-nsdm40-20261012.basis: Names National Underwater Reconnaissance Program among Defense programs subject to 40 Committee policy review and mission approval.

navy-nuro-scholarly-20261012.scope: NURO passage, authorship and reference chain only; not independent inspection of the cited 1998 book or original charter.
navy-nuro-scholarly-20261012.basis: Keith C. Clarke dates NURO to 1969, expressly citing Sontag and Drew, Blind Man’s Bluff (1998), pp. 82–83.

navy-nuwc-150-20261012.basis: 1869 Torpedo Station and 1951, 1966, 1970 and 1992 successor names.

navy-oni-nara-20261012.basis: ONI established by General Order 292 on March 23, 1882; later organizational transfers.

navy-oni-nmio-2022-20261012.basis: ONI and NMIO are distinct roles sharing a leader; NMIC is the Suitland facility.

navy-onr-guide-20261012.basis: ONT created 1980, OAT 1990, joined ONR in 1993; guide is not comprehensive.

navy-onr-nara-20261012.basis: ORI created May 15, 1945; ONR replaced it in 1946. NRL administrative relationship.

navy-op20g-nsa-20261012.scope: Title, disclaimer and Navy organizational section only; 104-page book joins two 1989 histories. Historical research, not a current NSA policy statement.
navy-op20g-nsa-20261012.basis: OP-20-G designation July 1922; new communications-intelligence Research Desk January 1924; March 11, 1935 reorganization as Communications Security Group.

navy-pax-history-20261012.scope: Article read; official chronology gives January 1, 1992 for NAWCAD, whereas an unread contemporary-newsletter lead gives January 2. Month precision retained pending charter resolution.
navy-pax-history-20261012.basis: NAS commissioned April 1, 1943; NATC June 16, 1945; NAWCAD January 1992; NAVAIR headquarters at Pax 1997.

navy-point-loma-history-20261012.scope: Overview and wartime sections; online excerpt updated after 1992 although original NOSC TD 1940 was published September 1990. Not treated as a verbatim 1990 document.
navy-point-loma-history-20261012.basis: NRSL June 1, 1940; UCDWR April 26, 1941; NOSC merger in 1977; NCCOSC establishment January 2, 1992.

navy-tusc-rename-20261012.basis: September 30, 2022 name change; IUSS fixed, mobile and deployable acoustic surveillance mission.

navy-usntps-history-20261012.basis: March 12, 1945 origin; developmental test-pilot, flight-officer and engineer education.

space-arpa-20261012.basis: DoD Directive 5105.15 established ARPA on 7 February 1958; its initial research areas included space technology, ballistic missile defense and solid propellants.

space-bmews-uewr-20261012.scope: Written description only; video not watched.
space-bmews-uewr-20261012.basis: Identifies Thule UEWR as former BMEWS Site 1. Describes 12 SWS missile-warning, missile-defense and secondary orbital-surveillance duties.

space-corona-release-20261012.scope: Relevant opening and release-history paragraphs inspected.
space-corona-release-20261012.basis: Clinton authorized declassification and public release of CORONA imagery on 22 February 1995; describes CORONA as first U.S. satellite imaging system, not first reconnaissance satellite of any kind.

space-darpa-names-20261012.basis: ARPA was renamed DARPA in 1972, reverted to ARPA in 1993 and became DARPA again in 1996. These are names of the same institution.

space-delta2-2021-20261012.basis: Delta 2 activated on 24 July 2020. Radar/optical sensors and missile-warning contributors provide orbital-awareness data. Identifies Eglin AN/FPS-85 and the Kwajalein Space Fence.

space-naca-20261012.basis: A Naval Appropriations rider created NACA on 3 March 1915 for aeronautical research.

space-nasa-operations-20261012.scope: Specific establishment/operations and employee/laboratory transfer text inspected.
space-nasa-operations-20261012.basis: NASA began operations 1 October 1958 after July Space Act; NACA personnel and laboratories formed nucleus. Distinct law and operational dates.

space-nasa-records-20261012.scope: Opened and read administrative history and NACA transfer paragraphs; not the entire finding aid or underlying statutory instruments.
space-nasa-records-20261012.basis: NASA was established as an independent agency by the Space Act on July 29, 1958. Its functions include aeronautical research, space-vehicle development and exploration. NACA functions transferred to NASA.

space-nasa-uap-overview-20261012.scope: Opened and read the announcement, scope, report-date and meeting sections of the current overview.
space-nasa-uap-overview-20261012.basis: NASA announced the independent study on June 9, 2022, focusing on available data, future collection and scientific understanding. Its team met publicly May 31, 2023 and issued its report September 14, 2023.

space-norad-history-20261012.basis: NORAD began operations on 12 September 1957 and received formal binational recognition on 12 May 1958. Operations moved to Cheyenne Mountain in 1966; maritime warning was added in 2006.

space-nro-1961-20261012.scope: Full letter and the co-directorship caveat read.
space-nro-1961-20261012.basis: Original document describes a covert NRO and its management of the National Reconnaissance Program. The editorial note states that the proposed co-directorship never went into effect.

space-nro-1992-20261012.scope: Downloaded and visually inspected entire scanned page.
space-nro-1992-20261012.basis: Deputy Secretary Don Atwood announces existence, historical mission and reporting arrangements; expressly says no other NRO information has been declassified.

space-nro-almanac-20261012.scope: Relevant introductory program and organizational passages and dated chronology inspected. Final review also inspected printed pp. 31–34 for imagery declassification and program-material release distinctions.
space-nro-almanac-20261012.basis: Supports CORONA authorization and first photographic recovery, GRAB launch, GAMBIT and HEXAGON first missions, alphabet-office roles and 1974/1992 closures. Records 2000 approval and 2002 transfer of some KH-7/KH-9 imagery, separately from 2011 program declassification/release; QUILL documents released July 9, 2012.

space-nro-history-20261012.scope: Targeted text passages and chronology inspected, not entire volume.
space-nro-history-20261012.basis: Supports the alphabet offices, 1962/1963 agreements, GRAB and POPPY chronology, Program D closure, QUILL and disclosure dates. Conflicts in the co-directorship and A-12 passages are explicitly excluded from adopted claims.

space-nro-public-1971-20261012.scope: Downloaded and visually inspected pages 1–2 of five-page redacted memorandum.
space-nro-public-1971-20261012.basis: CIA review identifies Benjamin Welles New York Times article of 22 January 1971 as the first public-domain NRO mention and describes subsequent public references. It says the article wrongly placed NRO within DIA.

space-nro-query-1973-20261012.scope: Downloaded and visually inspected both pages.
space-nro-query-1973-20261012.basis: Authorizes OASD public affairs, only in response to direct inquiry, to acknowledge an NRO administered by a senior Air Force civilian. Does not prove that the authorized reply was issued. Stamp approves release 2003-09-30, distinct from original cable date.

space-parcae-speech-20261012.scope: Downloaded PDF and visually inspected all three embedded prepared-speech pages; HTML omits the scanned material.
space-parcae-speech-20261012.basis: Prepared remarks announce PARCAE declassification: first launch in 1976, final improved-version launch in 1996, final satellite operating until 2008. Describes NRL/NRO lineage, low Earth orbit and foreign-fleet ELINT. The 2023 speech is reproduced in a 2026 volume of a March 2025 hearing.
space-parcae-speech-20261012.accessStatus: inspected-local-scan; web PDF too large to parse

space-parcs-20261012.scope: Relevant radar/operator and renaming text read.
space-parcs-20261012.basis: Identifies 10 SWS, a Delta 4 unit, as PARCS operator. Describes warning and surveillance data supplied to NORAD and USSPACECOM; the installation rename did not change the radar mission.

space-pave-paws-20261012.scope: Relevant mission and radar paragraphs inspected.
space-pave-paws-20261012.basis: Cape Cod PAVE PAWS/UEWR detects ICBM s/SLBM s and contributes orbital tracking/collision-avoidance data;6 SWS is a Delta 4 unit in this 2021 record.

space-poppy-release-20261012.scope: Release text on first page inspected; attached photographs not required for claims.
space-poppy-release-20261012.basis: NRO, NSA and NRL publicly announce declassification and recognition of POPPY, a GRAB successor for radar ELINT and ocean surveillance, with seven launches 1962–1971.

space-radar-context-20261012.basis: A dated 2018 description identifies PARCS, PAVE PAWS, upgraded early-warning radars and COBRA DANE, with missile-warning, defense and situational-awareness roles.

space-samso-1979-henderson-20261012.scope: Opened and read the relevant career paragraph and as-of statement.
space-samso-1979-henderson-20261012.basis: The official biography explicitly says SAMSO was redesignated Space Division in October 1979. It supports month precision, not an exact day.

space-samso-1979-hendricks-20261012.scope: Opened and read the mission, redesignation and as-of paragraphs.
space-samso-1979-hendricks-20261012.basis: The biography describes Space Division as responsible for research, development and acquisition of U.S. space systems, and dates the SAMSO redesignation to October 1979.

space-sda-about-20261012.scope: Relevant establishment and architecture-mission text inspected as of the review date.
space-sda-about-20261012.basis: Agency established 12 March 2019; develops and fields proliferated space capabilities. Acquisition agency, not a military service or combatant command.

space-sda-transfer-20261012.scope: Transfer date and organizational rationale inspected.
space-sda-transfer-20261012.basis: SDA transferred to the USSF on 1 October 2022, retaining its acquisition approach.

space-spacecom-1985-20261012.scope: Speech heading and relevant paragraphs read; not full collected volume.
space-spacecom-1985-20261012.basis: Contemporary activation remarks establish 23 September 1985 as the original command activation date and explain the unified military-space support mission.

space-spacecom-2002-20261012.scope: Relevant original testimony and hearing date inspected.
space-spacecom-2002-20261012.basis: Ellis testifies that UCP Change 1 combined functions of the former U.S. Space Command and U.S. Strategic Command on 1 October 2002.

space-spacecom-2019-20261012.scope: Caption and relevant surrounding article inspected.
space-spacecom-2019-20261012.basis: Official caption distinguishes September 1985 formation, 2002 disestablishment and 29 August 2019 reestablishment.

space-ssc-2021-20261012.scope: Relevant stand-up and organizational paragraphs inspected.
space-ssc-2021-20261012.basis: SMC was redesignated SSC on 13 August 2021 as a USSF field command with acquisition, launch, test, checkout and sustainment responsibilities.

space-ssn-2023-20261012.basis: Describes SSN as a worldwide radar/optical network tracking artificial orbital objects. The dated account identifies 18 SDS as its tasking unit, and 20 SPSS as operator of Eglin radar and Space Fence.

space-usaf-space-history-20261012.scope: Downloaded scan; title and pages 71–74 visually inspected.
space-usaf-space-history-20261012.basis: WDD July 1954, AFBMD June 1957, 1961 split, 1967 SAMSO, AFSPC 1982 and subsequent sensor/launch transfers, later acquisition names, and DSP missile-warning use in Desert Storm.

space-ussf-2019-20261012.basis: USSF was established on 20 December 2019 within the Department of the Air Force to organize, train and equip space forces. AFSPC was established on 1 September 1982; its redesignation was an initial step in standing up the new service.
